Free image via[Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/bridge-in-park-covered-with-snow-in-wintertime-5357766/)


While we look forward to new beginnings, the start of a new year also brings the magic of winter to New York City. Winter in NYC has a character all its own, with crisp temperatures, cozy moments, and a unique energy throughout the city. If you’ve never experienced a New York winter before, get ready to embrace a season unlike any other.


Of course, other regions may experience lower temperatures and heavier snowfall, but winter in NYC has its own unique charm. With so much of the city accessible by foot and public transportation, you’ll have plenty of opportunities to experience the city up close while staying active and embracing the crisp winter air. Bundle up, grab your coat, and get ready to explore.


Whether you’re trudging through ice and snow to reach the subway, hoping to luck out and grab a taxi, or waiting for the bus in blizzards, navigating NYC’s frozen streets and intersections sometimes piled eight feet high with snow is a feat unto itself. And when that wind rips, the real feel can be 15 or 20 degrees lower than the actual temperature.


Now that you know what makes winter in New York so unique, it’s time to experience it for yourself. Are you ready for a New York winter? Here’s our guide to surviving a NYC winter.


## How to Dress for Winter in NYC


Free image via[Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/family-enjoying-snowy-winter-day-together-30973827/)


A down coat will save you in January and February when the city is at its coldest and windiest. Invest in a quality coat that will last for years. You’ll need waterproof boots to travel through the ice and snow, so be prepared to carry stylish shoes in your city bag or keep a pair at the office. A pair of rubber boots will also come in handy, especially when the snow melts, and turn into puddles when the temperatures start getting warmer.


Accessories are a must too. Choose scarves that are long enough to knot and wrap around your neck several times to create a barrier between your skin and the wind. A lined wool hat that covers your ears, earmuffs, and mittens are extras that you’ll need to include in your winter wardrobe for NYC. Tech-friendly gloves will be your best friend while you spend time on the streets of New York. You won’t have to remove the gloves to text friends or return those pertinent work emails.


Other great winter items would be a wool dress coat for special occasions, warm sweaters, thick socks, and sunglasses to protect your eyes from freezing winds that can dry them out or make them tear. And if you’re going to spend a lot of time standing outside, you might want to invest in thermal underwear and foot and hand warmers. These are all New York winter essentials that will provide you with some sort of relief in the blistering cold.


## What You Should Know About Snow Removal in NYC


Free image via[Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/photo-of-people-walking-near-building-IVMh3NJkEG8)


Unless you own a home in New York City, you shouldn’t be responsible for shoveling or maintaining sidewalks. Your super and building staff will oversee clearing your walkway so that it’s clean and safe to walk on. If you do own a home in NYC, be sure to invest in a good shovel and salt ahead of time. Running to the store before a storm can have you fighting for the last of the snow removal materials!


When New York gets a lot of snow (a foot or more) or several snowstorms within a short period, snow tends to pile up quickly. There’s nowhere to put the snow until it melts, so visibility at intersections and the simple act of walking gets challenging. Keep this in mind as navigating NYC in these conditions might add time to your typical commute.


## Where to Park your Car in NYC During the Winter


When snow arrives in NYC, alternate-side parking rules are often suspended, which means you may not have to move your car for several days. However, that doesn’t mean your car will be easy to get to. After a major snowfall, your vehicle may be buried under snow or boxed in by piles of snow pushed aside by plows. Be prepared to spend some time digging it out before you can hit the road again.


While owning a car in the city has its merits, it can also be a bit of a hassle in wintertime. You might consider parking in a lot (if you don’t already) or opting for[vehicle storage](https://www.cubesmart.com/vehicle-storage/) from December through March to avoid digging out and moving your car when alternate side parking is in effect, not to mention finding a place to park when half a block is occupied by snow banks. Then, there are all the other New Yorkers vying for spaces too. And in NYC, there are more cars than spaces.


## Transit and Walking Tips


Free image via[Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/times-square-in-a-snowstorm-with-neon-signs-y4-OybV4To4)


If you’re walking, give yourself extra time and wear shoes with solid traction, as black ice and slushy corners can turn sidewalks into slipping hazards. Stick to well-cleared routes, watch for refrozen curb-cut puddles, and use handrails on stairs and at subway entrances.


Before you head out, check real-time transit alerts; snow and freezing rain often slow trains and send buses on detours. Enter stations cautiously; platforms can be slick. Wait until the train stops fully before stepping toward the edge. If buses are rerouted, try a nearby subway line or walk a block or two to a better-plowed avenue.


## Tips for NYC Dog Owners in the Winter


Maintenance staff of apartment buildings sprinkle ice melt on sidewalks, and that salt can harm a dog’s paws. When walking dogs in the cold, avoid any treated areas or be sure that your pup wears booties. Beyond the necessary precautions for your dog’s feet, pooches love to romp and play in the snow, so that’s yet another reason to dress warmly for the great outdoors. If your dog doesn’t have thick fur, purchase a winter jacket to keep your furry friend warm too.


## Be Ready for the Snow and Ice to Melt


Even as winter begins to wind down, snow and ice can stick around in NYC. When temperatures rise from around freezing into the upper 40s or 50s, accumulated snow can melt quickly, sometimes creating puddles and localized flooding. Large snowbanks left behind by plows can linger along streets and sidewalks, and shaded patches of snow and ice may remain well into April.


## What to do During a NYC Winter


There are many reasons why locals[love living in New York City](https://www.cubesmart.com/blog/city-guides/nyc/moving-guide/11-reasons-to-love-living-in-new-york-city/) including wintertime. During the winter you can enjoy ice skating at Rockefeller Center or Bryant Park, stroll through snowy Central Park, and warm up with dumplings in Chinatown or ramen in the East Village. On colder days, explore world-class museums like the Met or MoMA, catch a Broadway show, or browse the Strand. For a local feel, wander DUMBO’s cobblestone streets, take the Staten Island Ferry at sunset, or sample global cuisine in Flushing. Whether you’re outdoors or staying cozy inside, NYC shines in winter.
